args.body:
PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

DEVIATION REPORT
Analyze Counterparty Markup of Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement

Matter: data-privacy-cybersecurity — Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement
Practice Area: Data Privacy & Cybersecurity
Deliverable: deviation-report.docx

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

This deviation report compares the counterparty's latest markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement against (i) our original draft, (ii) the firm's negotiation playbook, (iii) the transfer impact summary prepared by the cross-functional privacy and security team, and (iv) the partner instructions issued on this matter. The purpose of this report is to document every material deviation introduced by the counterparty, evaluate each against our negotiating position and regulatory obligations, and recommend an accept / reject / counter position for each.

The counterparty markup introduces a total of deviations across the agreement's core provision categories: representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination. Several of these deviations are beneficial or neutral, but a significant number shift risk away from the counterparty and onto our client and must be rejected or countered. The markup also surfaces gaps between the original draft and the transfer impact summary that require alignment before execution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. SCOPE, MATERIALS REVIEWED, AND METHODOLOGY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Materials Reviewed

This report was prepared by reviewing the following operative materials:

  • Our Original Draft — the baseline Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement circulated to the counterparty prior to the markup.
  • Counterparty Markup — the counterparty's tracked changes to the original draft forming the subject of this analysis.
  • Firm Playbook — the data-privacy-cybersecurity negotiation playbook setting out preferred positions, fallback positions, and non-negotiables for cross-border data transfer agreements.
  • Transfer Impact Summary — the cross-functional assessment of the data flows, categories of personal data in scope, countries of transfer, applicable transfer mechanisms (e.g., Standard Contractual Clauses / SCCs, adequacy decisions), and resulting residual risk.
  • Partner Instructions — the engagement partner's directives setting the acceptable risk envelope, commercial priorities, and required approvals for any departure from playbook positions.

B. Methodology

Each counterparty change was catalogued against the corresponding original draft provision, scored for risk and alignment with the playbook and transfer impact summary, and assigned a recommended disposition (Accept, Reject, or Counter). Deviations are organized below by agreement section.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. DEVIATION ANALYSIS BY PROVISION CATEGORY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

CATEGORY 1 — REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES

1.1 Counterparty clarification of "personal data" definition
  • Original draft: Defined "personal data" by reference to the law of the exporting country.
  • Counterparty markup: Expanded the definition to a purpose-conferred, activity-based definition aligned with the GDPR's broad scope, capturing data relating to an identified or identifiable natural person regardless of jurisdiction of the data subject.
  • Playbook position: The playbook endorses the broad GDPR-style definition as the default for cross-border transfers.
  • Transfer impact summary: Confirms that the majority of the in-scope data subjects are located in the EU/EEA, so a broad definition is appropriate.
  • Assessment: ALIGNED with playbook and transfer impact summary.
  • Recommended disposition: ACCEPT.

1.2 Addition of representation on lawfulness of processing and data minimization
  • Original draft: Contained a limited representation that data was collected in compliance with applicable law.
  • Counterparty markup: Added an affirmative representation that the exporting controller shall only transfer personal data that has been processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner, and that the data transferred is limited to what is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of the transfer.
  • Playbook position: Mirrors standard market practice in SCC-based appendices; the playbook supports including it provided the representation is mutual.
  • Assessment: Neutral-to-favorable. Consider whether mutuality applies to imports as well as exports.
  • Recommended disposition: ACCEPT with conforming mutuality language extending the same obligations to the importing party.

1.3 Counterparty addition of a "no sensitive data" carve-out representation
  • Original draft: Addressed sensitive/special category data through a schedule.
  • Counterparty markup: Introduced a representation that no special categories of personal data (sensitive data) are included within the scope of transfers, narrowing the operative scope and effectively shifting burden onto our client to confirm the absence of such data.
  • Transfer impact summary: Expressly identifies that the current data flows INCLUDE special category data (e.g., health-related data of certain data subjects).
  • Assessment: CONFLICTS with the transfer impact summary. If accepted, this representation would be false on the client's present facts, creating immediate misrepresentation exposure.
  • Recommended disposition: REJECT. Counter with a representation acknowledging that special category data is in scope and subject to the additional safeguards required under the applicable transfer mechanism and Article 9 GDPR analysis.

CATEGORY 2 — COVENANTS

2.1 Counterparty security safeguards covenant downgrade
  • Original draft: Required the importer to implement organizational, technical and physical security measures consistent with a "state of the art" standard, and to maintain a documented information security program.
  • Counterparty markup: Downgraded the standard to "industry standard" measures, deleted the documented program requirement, and removed the obligation to promptly notify the exporter of any confirmed security incident affecting transferred data.
  • Playbook position: The playbook treats "state of the art," a documented security program, and timely incident notification as non-negotiables for any cross-border arrangement involving the data categories in scope.
  • Transfer impact summary: Flags heightened sensitivity of the in-scope data and recommends retention of robust security covenants.
  • Assessment: MATERIAL DEVIATION. Downgrades security standards, deletes the program requirement, and eliminates incident notification — all inconsistent with the playbook and the transfer impact summary.
  • Recommended disposition: REJECT. Counter to restore "state of the art," the documented program, and a defined incident-notification window (e.g., 72 hours per GDPR breach-notification expectations).

2.2 Sub-processor / onward transfer approval covenant narrowed
  • Original draft: Required the exporting controller's prior written consent for any sub-processor or onward transfer, with a right to object.
  • Counterparty markup: Replaced prior written consent with prior written "notice," allowing the importer to engage sub-processors absent an objection within a short window, and broadened the permitted onward-transfer categories.
  • Playbook position: The playbook requires prior written consent for sub-processor appointments and restricts onward transfers to permitted jurisdictions/recipients.
  • Assessment: MATERIAL DEVIATION. Weakens the exporter's control over downstream data flows.
  • Recommended disposition: REJECT. Counter with prior written consent and a defined sub-processor list and change process.

2.3 Deletion/return covenant qualified by "business records" retention carve-out
  • Original draft: Required the importer to delete or return all personal data at the end of the term, and to certify deletion.
  • Counterparty markup: Qualified the obligation by permitting the importer to retain copies required for compliance with its own legal obligations and by providing that certification may be deferred indefinitely pending third-party audit.
  • Playbook position: Permits a narrow legal-retention carve-out, but requires a bounded retention schedule and a firm deletion-certification deadline.
  • Assessment: DEVIATION. The indefinite and unbounded retention carve-out undermines the deletion commitment.
  • Recommended disposition: COUNTER — narrow the retention carve-out to a defined, time-limited schedule and require deletion certification within a fixed period (e.g., 60 days).

CATEGORY 3 — CONDITIONS TO CLOSING

3.1 Counterparty addition of a "transfer mechanism in place" condition precedent
  • Original draft: Did not condition closing on the execution of separate transfer mechanism documentation.
  • Counterparty markup: Added a condition precedent requiring that, prior to any transfer, the parties execute valid SCCs (or an alternative approved transfer mechanism) reflecting the transfer impact summary.
  • Playbook position: The playbook endorses executing SCC annexes as a condition to the initial transfer.
  • Assessment: ALIGNED with playbook and transfer impact summary; lawful-basis hygiene.
  • Recommended disposition: ACCEPT, with conforming language ensuring the SCCs and this agreement are consistent and cross-referenced.

3.2 Counterparty deletion of the "no undischarged obligations" closing condition
  • Original draft: Contained a closing condition that neither party have any undischarged obligations, including indemnity obligations, that would prevent performance.
  • Counterparty markup: Deleted this condition.
  • Playbook position: Retaining this condition is standard and low-cost.
  • Assessment: MINOR DEVIATION; removal weakens closing protection.
  • Recommended disposition: COUNTER to reinstate, or accept only if the operative closing conditions remain adequate.

CATEGORY 4 — INDEMNIFICATION

4.1 Counterparty addition of capped and mutual indemnity for third-party claims
  • Original draft: Contained indemnification for breach of the representations, warranties and covenants, but with amounts uncapped and one-way in our client's favor.
  • Counterparty markup: Converted the indemnity to a mutual, capped structure — limiting each party's indemnity liability to a fixed multiple of fees and imposing a claims-window limitation.
  • Playbook position: Capped mutual indemnities are acceptable for a data transfer context, but the cap must reflect risk of regulatory fines and the sensitivity of the data in scope.
  • Transfer impact summary: Notes that regulatory exposure (fines and supervisory-authority actions) materially exceeds the counterparty's proposed cap.
  • Assessment: MATERIAL DEVIATION. The proposed cap is too low relative to the regulatory exposure identified in the transfer impact summary and would leave the client under-compensated for the importer's breaches.
  • Recommended disposition: COUNTER — increase the cap and add a carve-out from the cap for breaches caused by (a) wilful misconduct or fraud and (b) fines imposed by a supervisory authority arising from the importer's non-compliance.

4.2 Counterparty addition of a limitation on consequential damages
  • Original draft: Silent on consequential damages.
  • Counterparty markup: Added a mutual waiver of indirect, special, incidental and consequential damages.
  • Playbook position: A mutual consequential-damages waiver is market standard for commercial agreements and generally acceptable.
  • Assessment: Neutral-to-acceptable; standard market term.
  • Recommended disposition: ACCEPT, subject to confirming the waiver does not extend to third-party regulatory claims that should remain covered by the indemnity.

CATEGORY 5 — TERMINATION RIGHTS

5.1 Counterparty addition of termination "for convenience" right
  • Original draft: Permitted termination only for material breach (with cure) and insolvency.
  • Counterparty markup: Added a right for the importing party to terminate for convenience upon 30 days' notice.
  • Playbook position: The playbook generally resists for-convenience termination in data transfer arrangements given the regulatory continuity obligations and the practical difficulty of winding down in-scope data flows on short notice.
  • Transfer impact summary: Confirms re-routing or cessation of the affected flows within 30 days would not be feasible for the categories of data in scope.
  • Assessment: MATERIAL DEVIATION. A 30-day for-convenience termination is inconsistent with the playbook and the transfer impact summary's operational reality.
  • Recommended disposition: REJECT. If forced to concede any early-termination right, counter with a longer notice period (e.g., 90 days) coupled with a transition/wind-down obligation to ensure continuity and compliant cessation of processing.

5.2 Counterparty suspension of processing upon 10 days' notice for alleged regulatory non-compliance
  • Original draft: Required the parties to cooperate and, absent cure, resolve disputes through the specified mechanism before any unilateral cessation.
  • Counterparty markup: Allowed the importing party to unilaterally suspend processing on 10 days' notice whenever it asserts, in its reasonable discretion, that the exporter's processing violates applicable law.
  • Playbook position: Unilateral discretionary suspension by a party in a data-flow relationship is disfavored as it risks business disruption and is inconsistent with the cooperation regime.
  • Assessment: MATERIAL DEVIATION. Grants the counterparty a broad unilateral lever without a defined standard or cure/cooperation step.
  • Recommended disposition: COUNTER — require a good-faith objective basis, prior notice, an opportunity to cure, and escalation to the designated dispute-resolution mechanism before any suspension.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. CROSS-CUTTING ISSUES AND OBSERVATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Conflict Between Counterparty Markup and Transfer Impact Summary
   The markup's "no sensitive data" representation (Section 1.3 above) directly contradicts the transfer impact summary's identification of special-category data in the in-scope flows. This is the single most consequential inconsistency in the markup and must be resolved before any execution. Accepting that representation would create false-representation exposure for the client on current facts.

B. Gaps Between Original Draft and Transfer Impact Summary
   The transfer impact summary identifies an EU/EEA concentration of data subjects and the presence of special-category data, but the original draft did not fully operationalize these facts (e.g., no bespoke sensitive-data safeguards annex, no explicit SCC Annex references). The counterparty markup presents an opportunity to conform the agreement to the summary, but the markup's chosen mechanisms are — in several instances — risk-shifting rather than gap-filling.

C. Missing Negotiating Priorities Flagged in Partner Instructions
   The partner instructions emphasize (i) preserving state-of-the-art security and prompt incident notice, (ii) adequate indemnity cover relative to regulatory exposure, and (iii) retaining operational control over sub-processors and onward transfers. Each of these priorities is materially eroded by the markup as drafted and should be defended on the dispositions recommended above.

D. Alignment With Firm Playbook Non-Negotiables
   Under the playbook, the following are non-negotiables that the counterparty markup has attempted to dilute:
     • "State of the art" security standard and documented information security program (2.1)
     • Prior written consent for sub-processor appointments and onward transfers (2.2)
     • Adequate indemnity cap with fraud/wilful-misconduct and regulatory-fine carve-outs (4.1)
     • No for-convenience termination inconsistent with regulatory continuity obligations (5.1)
   These items should not be conceded absent express partner approval.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. SUMMARY TABLE OF DEVIATIONS AND RECOMMENDED DISPOSITIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

  #   Provision                                        Disposition
  ──  ────────────────────────────────────────────     ──────────
  1.1 Personal data definition expansion                ACCEPT
  1.2 Lawfulness & minimization representation          ACCEPT (add mutuality)
  1.3 "No sensitive data" representation                REJECT
  2.1 Security covenant downgrade                       REJECT (state of the art)
  2.2 Sub-processor/onward transfer notice vs consent   REJECT (prior written consent)
  2.3 Deletion/return retention carve-out               COUNTER (bounded schedule)
  3.1 Transfer mechanism condition precedent            ACCEPT
  3.2 Deletion of undischarged-obligations condition    COUNTER (reinstate)
  4.1 Cap on indemnity                                  COUNTER (raise cap + carve-outs)
  4.2 Consequential damages waiver                      ACCEPT
  5.1 For-convenience termination                       REJECT (or counter w/ 90-day + wind-down)
  5.2 Unilateral suspension right                       COUNTER (objective basis + cure)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

  1. Address the sensitive-data representational conflict (1.3) at the outset, as it is disqualifying under current facts and requires either a compensating safeguard annex or an amended representation.
  2. Return a consolidated redline reflecting the dispositions above, prioritizing the playbook non-negotiables (security, sub-processor control, indemnity cap, termination).
  3. Align the final agreement with the transfer impact summary (SCC Annexes, sensitive-data safeguards, data-flow schedule).
  4. Obtain partner sign-off on any departure from a "REJECT" or playbook non-negotiable position.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. CONCLUSION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

The counterparty markup, while containing several acceptable or beneficial clarifications, materially shifts risk onto our client across the security, sub-processing control, indemnification, and termination categories. The markup also introduces a direct conflict with the transfer impact summary on special-category data. This report recommends acceptance of four deviations, rejection of four, and counters on four, consistent with the firm playbook, the transfer impact summary, and the partner instructions. Execution should not proceed until the identified material deviations are resolved and the agreement is conformed to the transfer impact summary.

Respectfully submitted,
Deal Team — Data Privacy & Cybersecurity
